subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Sonali asked, “Sharmila, how did the science model go so wrong?” and Sharmila laughed. “Okay, listen. Our model volcano was due on Friday, and on Monday I sat and imagined it: paper mould one evening, paint the next, done by Wednesday. In my head nothing ever went wrong. So I started Tuesday night. The glue took a whole day to dry. The printer ran out of ink. The paint I wanted was finished at the shop, and I hadn't thought of any of that. Last year the same kind of project took me five days, not three, and I completely ignored that. I handed in a half-painted volcano on Friday and told myself it was a design choice.” 😅

qa.q: On which night did Sharmila start the model volcano?
qa.a: Sharmila started the volcano on Tuesday night.

qa.q: Why does Sharmila laugh while telling the story?
qa.a: Sharmila is laughing at the mistake and feeling a little embarrassed: the plan imagined everything going smoothly and ignored how last year's project had gone.

qa.q: What could Sharmila try next time before choosing a start date?
qa.a: Look at how long a similar project really took last year, and start earlier with time for glue drying and shop trips.

qa.q: What might Sonali be thinking as Sharmila tells this?
qa.a: Sonali is probably curious and amused, and perhaps recognising the same habit in Sonali's own projects.

grounding: A teenager estimates a project by imagining everything going smoothly and starts late as a result.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: I'm Irfan, and I sit behind Pranav in history. When our teacher announced the essay on Thursday, Pranav told me, “Two evenings, easy. I know the topic.” I said nothing, because I remembered the map project in September, which he'd said would take one night and which took six days. On Sunday night Pranav was still gathering sources, and the second evening was gone before the introduction was done. I saw him on Monday morning, writing the conclusion on the school bus with his notebook on his knees. I don't know what he was thinking. He looked tired, but he also said, “It'll be fine.” The teacher gave it a mark he didn't seem to like.

qa.q: How many evenings did Pranav say the essay would take?
qa.a: Pranav said the essay would take two evenings.

qa.q: What might Pranav have been feeling on the school bus on Monday?
qa.a: Pranav seemed tired and perhaps worried, though “It'll be fine” suggests hopeful confidence; Irfan cannot be sure about Pranav's inner state.

qa.q: What could Pranav do before the next essay?
qa.a: Look back at how long the map project and this essay really took, and plan the start date from that instead of from the best-case picture.

qa.q: Why did Irfan say nothing about the map project?
qa.a: Irfan may have felt awkward correcting a classmate, and wanted to avoid sounding critical, so kept quiet.

grounding: A teenager estimates a project from the ideal story and starts late, seen by a classmate.
